title: Dash: knowledge graphs, MCP limits and DSPy
problem: Scaling an AI search product exposed context bloat, latency in MCP-based agents and unmanageable prompts.
depth: Candid lessons and rejected alternatives; few quantitative results
technologies_stated: LLM-as-judge (an OpenAI o3 upgrade is mentioned)
facts: Tool definitions and returned content consume context; Dropbox caps context at about 100,000 tokens because quality degrades beyond it.
Some MCP-based agents took up to 45 seconds for a simple query versus seconds with direct index access.
Mitigations include one 'super tool' over the index instead of many retrieval tools, storing large results outside the model context and sub-agents with narrower tool sets.

A graph database was tried and rejected for latency, query pattern and hybrid retrieval reasons; graphs are built asynchronously and compressed into bundles that go through the normal chunk and embed pipeline.
Index-based retrieval was chosen over federated retrieval for connector coverage, preprocessing and speed, at the cost of engineering effort, storage and freshness management.
DSPy is used to optimise prompts against evals, starting with judge prompts; about 30 prompts are edited by 5-15 engineers.
interpretations: Federated MCP access is attractive for speed of integration but shifts quality and latency to each external system.
unknown: Knowledge graph schema and bundle construction

decisions.alternatives: Federated retrieval via MCP connectors to each app
decisions.reasoning: Source lists connector access, preprocessing, offline ranking and speed in favour of the index, and cost and freshness against.

decisions.selected: Single super tool over the index
decisions.reasoning: Source cites context cost and tool selection quality.

decisions.selected: Graph summarised into bundles in the existing retrieval pipeline
decisions.reasoning: Source states graph database was rejected for latency, query pattern and hybrid retrieval difficulty.
Source states preference for generating prompts from goals.

review_exercise: You are told to expose 40 enterprise APIs as MCP tools to one agent. Using this case, list the risks and redesign the tool surface.
lessons: Protocols do not remove latency and quality costs.
Prompt optimisation tooling pays off at scale.
adaptation: Directly relevant to exposing SAP APIs via MCP: scope servers narrowly and measure latency before scaling the tool count. Compare with CS-009. Independent analysis.
